stem: A client with schizophrenia repeatedly stops antipsychotic medication after symptoms improve. Which strategy best supports ongoing treatment adherence?

options.A: Explore why the client stops treatment, discuss benefits, adverse effects and preferences, and collaborate with the prescriber about a long-acting injectable if the client prefers it or adherence remains poor or uncertain.
options.B: Increase the antipsychotic dose automatically whenever the client reports feeling better, even when there is no evidence that the prescribed dose is ineffective.
options.C: Avoid discussing adverse effects because acknowledging medication problems generally makes clients less willing to continue treatment.
options.D: Postpone adherence planning until another relapse occurs because symptom improvement means maintenance antipsychotic treatment is no longer needed.

rationale: APA guidance recommends continuing antipsychotic treatment after symptoms improve and specifically suggests a long-acting injectable antipsychotic when a patient prefers it or has a history of poor or uncertain adherence. Treatment planning should remain patient-centered and adverse effects should be monitored rather than ignored. Therefore A is the best strategy. B changes dose without a clinical indication, C conflicts with monitoring and shared treatment planning, and D delays intervention despite an established adherence problem.
educational_objective: For a client with schizophrenia who repeatedly stops medication, address adherence barriers and preferences and recognize a long-acting injectable as an appropriate option when preferred or when adherence is poor or uncertain.
source_document_title: The American Psychiatric Association Practice Guideline for the Treatment of Patients With Schizophrenia, Third Edition
source_version_date: 2020 third edition; still listed by APA under Current Guidelines; APA schizophrenia guideline page updated September 12, 2025; rechecked 2026-08-16
source_locator: Guideline Statement Summary — Pharmacotherapy: continuation of antipsychotic treatment after symptom improvement; long-acting injectable recommendation for patient preference or history of poor/uncertain adherence
source_claim_supported: Patients whose schizophrenia symptoms improve should continue antipsychotic treatment; a long-acting injectable may be used when preferred or when adherence is poor or uncertain.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Printed p.10, Psychosocial Integrity — provide care and education for acute and chronic psychosocial health issues; use therapeutic communication and behavioral management techniques

source_original.stem: A client with schizophrenia repeatedly stops medication after symptoms improve. Which strategy best supports long-term adherence?

options.A: Explore barriers, provide collaborative education, and discuss long-acting injectable options when suitable
options.B: Increase the antipsychotic dose automatically whenever the client reports feeling better on treatment
options.C: Avoid discussing adverse effects because attention to side effects generally reduces medication adherence
options.D: Defer adherence planning until another relapse occurs because current symptom control is sufficient

source_original.rationale: Schizophrenia treatment guidance supports collaborative attention to adherence, patient preferences, treatment barriers, and use of long-acting injectable antipsychotics in appropriate patients, especially when adherence is a concern.
source_original.source_detail: APA schizophrenia guideline: treatment planning, adherence, shared decision-making, and long-acting injectable antipsychotic considerations; accessed 2026-08-14.

correction_summary: Kept the adherence construct but made the LAI indication exact (patient preference or poor/uncertain adherence), explicitly included adverse-effect discussion, replaced the generic source landing page with the exact schizophrenia guideline, added a claim-level locator, and reduced difficulty from hard to medium.

audit_findings.clinical_category: Schizophrenia — maintenance treatment and medication adherence
audit_findings.source_authority: APA current schizophrenia practice guideline; NCSBN 2026 Test Plan
audit_findings.currentness: APA currently lists Treatment of Patients with Schizophrenia (2020) under Current Guidelines; schizophrenia resource page last updated 2025-09-12.
audit_findings.claim_audit: The stem's recurrent stopping behavior establishes an adherence problem. APA supports continued maintenance antipsychotic treatment after improvement and LAI treatment when preferred or when adherence is poor/uncertain.

distractor_audit.A: Correct; directly aligns with patient-centered adherence management and the APA LAI indication.
distractor_audit.B: Incorrect; symptom improvement is not an indication for automatic dose escalation.
distractor_audit.C: Incorrect; APA recommends monitoring antipsychotic adverse effects and treatment decisions should account for patient preferences.
distractor_audit.D: Incorrect; APA recommends continued antipsychotic treatment after improvement, so an existing adherence problem should not be deferred until relapse.

audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: Only A simultaneously addresses the known adherence problem and uses an APA-supported treatment option without unsupported escalation or delay.
audit_findings.cueing: Options were rewritten to similar clinical specificity; the key is not identifiable by wording alone.
audit_findings.blueprint: NCSBN 2026 Psychosocial Integrity, printed p.10: care/education for psychosocial health issues and therapeutic/behavioral management.
audit_findings.independent_second_pass: Re-solved the final item without relying on the original key; rechecked APA current-guideline listing, maintenance-treatment and LAI statements, all four options, rationale, NCSBN p.10 mapping, second-answer risk, and unsupported precision. A remained uniquely correct.
